breathwork_parasympathetic.title: Breathwork techniques
breathwork_parasympathetic.description:
Breathing exercises have a long history, including yoga’s pranayama tradition. Today they are also used for relaxation and stress management.

Breathing and the heart interact: As the lungs fill and empty, their volume and pressure within the chest change. This affects blood returning to the heart. Lung stretch receptors also send signals through the vagus nerve to the brainstem. Together with central respiratory control and blood-pressure reflexes, these processes contribute to the normal increase in heart rate during inhalation and decrease during exhalation.

Gentle, slow breathing can amplify this rhythmic variation and influence vagal regulation of the heart. This may help some people settle. The connection concerns changes in lung volume during each breath, not larger lungs automatically providing better heart health. Breathe comfortably without forcing; stop if you feel dizzy.

sleep_optimization_recovery.title: Sleep optimization for recovery
sleep_optimization_recovery.description: This group brings together tips on sleep duration, regularity, environment, and bedtime preparation.

adaptogenic_herbs.title: Adaptogenic herbs
adaptogenic_herbs.description:
Adaptogens is a collective term for substances proposed to influence the body’s adaptation to stress. Several of these plants have a long history of traditional use, but the term does not describe a shared, proven effect.

The stress system links the brain, autonomic nervous system, and hormones. One component is the HPA axis: the hypothalamus and pituitary signal the adrenal glands to release hormones including cortisol. Researchers investigate whether particular plant extracts affect this signaling and cellular stress responses. Some ashwagandha trials have reported lower perceived stress and cortisol, but this does not mean that all adaptogens lower cortisol or restore hormonal balance.

Rhodiola, ashwagandha, and holy basil contain different compounds and require individual assessment. Proposed mechanisms partly derive from cell and animal experiments. Read each tip for human studies, personal reports, and safety; some products may also cause anxiety, sleep problems, or medication interactions.

medicinal_mushrooms.title: Medicinal mushrooms
medicinal_mushrooms.description:
History and tradition: Mushrooms have served as food and in healing traditions across cultures. In parts of East Asia, certain species have been used medicinally for hundreds of years. Reishi, also called lingzhi in China, has a long history of associations with vitality and longevity. These historical beliefs describe the tradition, not established effects.

From tradition to extracts: Historical preparations included dried material and decoctions. Today, products include powders, capsules, and extracts from fruiting bodies or mycelium. Comparisons matter: two products with the same mushroom name can differ in composition and concentration. A modern extract does not automatically match a traditional preparation.

What research examines: Interest includes polysaccharides such as beta-glucans and species-specific compounds. Researchers investigate immune signaling, the nervous system, and metabolism. Much of the evidence comes from cell and animal experiments; the extent and quality of human research differ between species and preparations.

In this group: Reishi, Lion’s Mane, Chaga, and Cordyceps have different profiles and require individual assessment. Read each tip for research, personal reports, and safety. A long tradition does not mean every preparation is effective or suitable for everyone.

probiotics_microbiota.title: Probiotics and gut microbiota
probiotics_microbiota.description: This group brings together tips on probiotics and specific microorganisms. Species, strains, and products need to be assessed individually.

fiber_microbiome.title: Fiber and microbiome health
fiber_microbiome.description:
Dietary fibers are not fully broken down by our own digestive enzymes. Some reach the large intestine and provide fuel for the microbiome – the community of microorganisms in the gut. Bacterial fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids including acetate, propionate, and butyrate. Butyrate is an important energy source for cells lining the colon and supports their function.

Different fibers have different roles. Fermentable fibers, such as inulin and resistant starch, can be used by different bacteria. Some gel-forming fibers bind water and influence stool consistency, while others mainly add bulk. Gel formation and fermentability are distinct properties; a fiber can have both. Total grams therefore do not describe the entire effect.

Cholesterol: Viscous, gel-forming fibers in particular can lower LDL cholesterol. Examples include beta-glucans from oats and barley and psyllium. Certain pectins and guar gum have also shown effects. The gel reduces intestinal reabsorption of bile acids, increasing their loss in stool. The liver then uses cholesterol to make new bile acids and may increase LDL uptake from the blood. Effects depend on factors including fiber viscosity, amount, and processing; soluble or fermentable fibers do not all have the same cholesterol-lowering effect.

Include a variety of whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts, and seeds. Bacteria can also cooperate by using one another’s breakdown products, but responses to a particular fiber vary between people. Increase intake gradually if unaccustomed, as fermentation also produces gas. Explore this group’s tips for more about fiber types and their individual targets.

sulfate.title: Sulfur from food
sulfate.description: Sulfur is part of the amino acids methionine and cysteine, which help build and maintain muscles, enzymes and keratin in hair and nails. Cysteine is also needed to produce glutathione, which protects cells against oxidative stress and participates in the body’s detoxification processes. In the liver, glutathione and sulfate help convert certain medicines and foreign substances into forms that can be excreted more easily. Sulfate is also needed for compounds in cartilage and other connective tissues.

amino_acids.title: Amino acids and related compounds
amino_acids.description: Amino acids are protein building blocks and also participate in signaling and metabolism. This group includes individual amino acids, combinations, and related compounds such as NAC. A biological role does not establish a need for supplementation; nutrition targets, evidence, and safety differ between tips.

light_infrared.title: Light and infrared heat
light_infrared.description:
This group covers red light, near infrared (NIR) and far infrared (FIR). They occupy different parts of the light spectrum and are used in different ways.

Red light and NIR are used in photobiomodulation, which investigates how light affects cellular signalling. FIR is used in infrared saunas, where heating and temperature regulation are central. Findings from an infrared sauna therefore cannot automatically be applied to a red light panel, or vice versa.

Effects depend on wavelength, dose, treatment area and equipment. Read each tip for mechanisms, evidence and safety; a possible effect in cell experiments is not the same as a proven health benefit in humans.

light_sleep.title: Light and sleep
light_sleep.description:
This group brings together tips on morning light, lighting hygiene and winding down with dim evening lighting. Together, they focus on giving the body clear signals for day and night.

Explore daylight during the day, dim evening lighting and how light habits interact with sleep timing. Each tip covers its own part and offers practical guidance.

nitric_oxide.title: Nitric oxide (NO)
nitric_oxide.description:
Nitric oxide (NO) is a short-lived signalling molecule produced at several sites in the body. Its roles include regulation of vascular tone. Location and amount matter; more NO in one place does not automatically mean better circulation throughout the body.

This group brings together tips on nasal and sinus NO, arginine, citrulline and dietary nitrate, alongside tips involving NO signalling as a possible mechanism, such as red light and vascular function in homocysteine metabolism. These pathways have different evidence bases and should not be treated as equivalent therapies.

The Viagra connection: NO activates soluble guanylate cyclase, increasing the messenger cGMP and relaxing vascular smooth muscle. Sildenafil, the active ingredient in Viagra, inhibits PDE5, which breaks down cGMP, thereby amplifying the NO signal during sexual stimulation. Its effect depends on activation of the body’s NO signalling; the medicine slows the breakdown of the messenger cGMP. Sildenafil must not be combined with nitrate medicines such as nitroglycerin because blood pressure can fall dangerously.
